title: Coda alla Vaccinara
subtitle: Roman slow-braised oxtail with celery, tomatoes, and spices
excerpt: Coda alla vaccinara is Rome's most celebrated offal dish and one of the great braises of Italian cooking: oxtail pieces slowly braised with celery, tomatoes, red wine, cloves, and a little cocoa, in the sweet-and-sour style that defines Roman stew cooking. It is a dish of the mattatoio quarter of Rome, made by the butchers and workers of the old slaughterhouse.
sourceNotes: Coda alla vaccinara is named for the vaccinari (cattlemen/butchers) of Testaccio, the Roman slaughterhouse district. It is the definitive Roman oxtail dish, documented in Ada Boni's La Cucina Romana (1929) and in Elizabeth David's Italian Food. The addition of cocoa, pine nuts, and raisins in some versions reflects Rome's sweet-and-sour (agrodolce) tradition. It requires a full day to cook properly.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in its sauce. Reheat gently. Improves after freezing and reheating.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made the day before and reheated gently. The sauce deepens overnight.

content.text: Oxtail takes 3 to 4 hours at a very low simmer to become tender. The meat must fall from the bone without effort. Celery is the defining vegetable in this dish -- use a large amount, added in two stages: some at the start for the soffritto, and a larger quantity in the last hour to keep a fresh celery flavour. The cocoa (used in small amounts) adds depth and a slight bitterness that balances the tomatoes.

items.prepNote: cut into pieces by the butcher
4 for the soffritto (finely diced), 4 for the second stage (cut into 5 cm pieces)

content.text: Heat {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil in a large heavy pan over high heat. Season {{oxtail}} oxtail pieces with {{salt-table}} salt and {{black-pepper}} pepper. Brown in batches on all sides, about 8 minutes per batch. Remove and set aside.

Reduce heat to medium. Add {{onion}} onion, {{carrot}} carrot, and the finely diced {{celery}} celery (4 sticks). Cook for 10 minutes. Add {{garlic}} garlic and {{cloves}} cloves and cook for 1 minute. Pour in {{red-wine}} wine and simmer for 3 minutes.

Add {{tinned-tomatoes}} tomatoes. Return the oxtail to the pan. The liquid should come about halfway up the meat -- add water if needed. Bring to a very gentle simmer, cover tightly, and cook over the lowest possible heat for 2 hours.

Add the remaining {{celery}} celery pieces (cut into 5 cm pieces). Stir in {{cocoa-powder}} cocoa, and {{pine-nuts}} pine nuts and {{raisins}} raisins if using. Cover and continue cooking for a further 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes, until the meat falls from the bone completely and the sauce is thick and dark. Taste for {{salt-table}} salt.

items.symptom: The oxtail is still tough after 3 hours
items.cause: Oxtail requires a very low, sustained simmer. Any bubbling that is too aggressive toughens the meat.
items.fix: Continue cooking at the lowest possible heat, covered. Add a splash of water if the sauce is reducing too fast. Oxtail can take 4 hours to become truly tender. The dish cannot be rushed.

content.text: Coda alla vaccinara comes from Testaccio, the old slaughterhouse quarter of Rome on the west bank of the Tiber. The vaccinari were the men who worked with cattle -- butchers, skinners, and workers of the mattatoio. They were paid partly in offal, the parts of the animal that the wealthy did not want, and developed a complete cuisine around the quinto quarto (fifth quarter) of the beast. Oxtail, tripe, liver, and kidney are all part of this tradition. Coda alla vaccinara is the most refined and celebrated dish of this group, and is now served in Rome's finest restaurants as well as in family kitchens.
